topic: Coroutine internals: CPS, state machines & Continuation

questions.question: On the JVM, what signature does the compiler actually generate for this function?
options: fun fetch(id: Int, $completion: Continuation<String>): Any?
fun fetch(id: Int): Deferred<String>
fun fetch(id: Int, callback: (String) -> Unit): Unit
fun fetch(id: Int, $completion: Continuation<String>): String
questions.explanation: The continuation-passing-style transform adds a `Continuation<T>` parameter that represents "the rest of the computation". The return type becomes `Any?` because the function either returns its real result directly or returns the special `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED` marker. It cannot be `String`, since a suspended call has no string to return yet.

questions.question: Marking a function `suspend` makes its body run on a background thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `suspend` only means the function may pause without blocking the thread; it says nothing about which thread runs it. The body runs on whatever dispatcher the calling coroutine uses, which may well be the main thread. To move work off the main thread you need `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` or similar.

questions.explanation: `launch` only schedules the child on runBlocking's single-threaded event loop, so the parent keeps running and prints A first. `yield()` suspends the parent and puts it at the back of the queue, letting the child print B before the parent resumes with C. The child does not run before A because nothing has suspended yet.

questions.question: Roughly how does the compiler implement the body of this function?
options: One continuation object with a `label`; a `when (label)` with 3 branches resumes each step
Three separate continuation classes chained together, one generated for each suspend call
A thread is parked at each suspend call and is woken again when the result arrives
Two nested callback lambdas are generated and the dispatcher invokes them in sequence
questions.explanation: The compiler turns the body into a single state machine: two suspension points give three states (start, after `user`, after `posts`), selected by a `label` stored in one continuation object. On resume, the function is re-entered and jumps to the right branch. It does not generate nested callbacks or park threads, which is why coroutines are cheap.

questions.question: While this coroutine is suspended inside `api.posts(user)`, where is the local variable `user` kept?
options: In a field of the function's continuation object, saved before suspending
On the thread's stack, which stays reserved for the coroutine until it resumes
In a ThreadLocal owned by the dispatcher that will resume the coroutine later
In the CoroutineContext, stored as an extra element keyed by the variable name
questions.explanation: When a coroutine suspends, its stack frame is gone: the thread returns to do other work. So the compiler "spills" live locals into fields of the generated continuation object and restores them on resume. The thread stack is not kept reserved; that is exactly what makes suspension non-blocking.

questions.question: Inside a generated state machine, how does a caller know whether a suspend function it just called actually suspended?
options: The callee returns the COROUTINE_SUSPENDED marker, which the caller passes up
The callee throws an internal SuspendException that each caller catches and rethrows
The dispatcher sets a flag on the Job, which the caller checks right after the call
It doesn't need to know: a call to a suspend function always suspends the caller
questions.explanation: A suspend function returns either its result (it completed without suspending, the fast path) or `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`. On the marker, the caller saves its state and also returns the marker, unwinding the stack; later the callee resumes the caller's continuation. Suspend calls often do not suspend at all, for example a cached value or a `withContext` that needs no switch.

questions.question: Which statements about `kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<T>` are true? Select all that apply.
options: It exposes a `context: CoroutineContext` property
Its single abstract function is `resumeWith(result: Result<T>)`
`resume(value)` and `resumeWithException(e)` are extensions built on `resumeWith`
Resuming a `suspendCoroutine` continuation twice is fine; the second call is ignored
It holds a reference to the thread on which the coroutine was started
questions.explanation: `Continuation` is just a context plus `resumeWith(Result<T>)`; `resume` and `resumeWithException` are convenience extensions. Resuming the same `suspendCoroutine` continuation twice throws `IllegalStateException` ("Already resumed"), it is not silently ignored. Continuations carry no thread; the dispatcher in the context decides where the coroutine resumes.

questions.question: When wrapping a callback API, why is `suspendCancellableCoroutine` usually preferred over `suspendCoroutine`?
options: It reacts to cancellation at once and lets you unregister in invokeOnCancellation
suspendCoroutine always resumes on the main thread while the cancellable one uses Dispatchers.IO
suspendCoroutine can't propagate errors; only the cancellable variant has resumeWithException
It resumes the coroutine on its own after a timeout when the callback never ends up being called
questions.explanation: With `suspendCoroutine`, a cancelled coroutine stays suspended until the callback fires, and the listener keeps a reference alive. `suspendCancellableCoroutine` resumes with `CancellationException` as soon as the job is cancelled and gives you `invokeOnCancellation` to cancel the request or remove the listener. Both support `resumeWithException`, and neither has a built-in timeout.

questions.question: A `suspend` function whose body never calls another suspending function still compiles into a state machine with a `label` field.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The compiler still adds the `Continuation` parameter, but it only generates a state machine when the body has suspension points. With none, the function simply runs and returns its value, and the IDE warns about a redundant `suspend` modifier. The state machine exists to remember where to resume, which is unnecessary if nothing can suspend.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
import kotlin.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.*

suspend fun answer(): Int = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    println("inside")
    cont.resume(42)
    println("after resume")
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println("start")
    println(answer())
    println("end")
}
options:
start
inside
after resume
42
end

start
inside
42
after resume
end

start
inside
42
end

start
inside
after resume
end
42
questions.explanation: The block passed to `suspendCoroutine` runs synchronously, so it prints inside, records the result on `resume(42)`, and keeps going to print after resume. `resume` does not jump back to the caller mid-block. Because the result was already set when the block returned, the call returns 42 without really suspending, and then end prints.
